title: Birds Fear Women More Than Men. Crows Never Forget Your Face
description: This week a study across five European countries found that city birds flee sooner from women than from men, and the scientists can't explain why. We count down five ways birds secretly read humans, from pigeons that see through disguises to crows that held a grudge for 17 years.
sources: ScienceDaily / British Ecological Society (22 Oct 2026) Birds are more afraid of women than men. Scientists have no idea why; Morelli et al., 'Sex matters: European urban birds flee approaching women sooner than approaching men', People and Nature, doi:10.1002/pan3.70226 — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261021231250.htm

University of Florida News (May 2009) Mockingbirds, no bird brains, can recognize a face in a crowd; Levey et al., PNAS — https://archive.news.ufl.edu/articles/2009/05/research-mockingbirds-no-bird-brains-can-recognize-a-face-in-a-crowd.html

Live Science (3 Jul 2011) Pigeons recognize human faces (Dalila Bovet, Univ. Paris Ouest Nanterre; Animal Cognition doi:10.1007/s10071-011-0420-7) — https://livescience.com/14895-pigeons-recognize-human-faces.html
NBC News Cosmic Log (2011) Don't mess with the magpies (Won Young Lee, Seoul National University; Animal Cognition) — https://www.nbcnews.com/science/cosmic-log/dont-mess-magpies-flna6c10403072
Sci.News (Mar 2016) Brown skuas can recognize individual humans; Lee et al., Animal Cognition — https://www.sci.news/biology/brown-skuas-recognize-individual-humans-03734.html

Popular Science (Jun 2012) How crows recognize individual humans, warn others (Marzluff & Angell, caveman and Cheney masks) — https://www.popsci.com/science/article/2012-06/how-crows-recognize-individual-humans-warn-others-and-are-basically-smarter-you/
Live Science (2011) also reports Auguste Bayern (University of Oxford, 2009): jackdaws respond to human eye cues — https://livescience.com/14895-pigeons-recognize-human-faces.html
Earth.com: Crows hold grudges for up to 17 years (Marzluff, University of Washington; 47 of 53 crows, peak 2013, silence Sept 2023) — https://earth.com/news/crows-hold-grudges-for-up-to-17-years

scenes.say: That bird in the park? It's watching you, and it might remember your face for years.

scenes.label: Not paranoia
scenes.say: Okay, so this isn't paranoia. Scientists have tested it with masks, lab coats, swapped hats, and even a trip to Antarctica.

scenes.label: Five bird secrets
scenes.say: Here's the plan. Five ways birds secretly read humans, counting down. Each one is weirder than the last.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: And stay to the very end. Because number one came out this week, and the scientists who found it say they can't explain it.

scenes.label: Who do they fear?
scenes.say: It's about who birds are most afraid of. And I promise, it's not who you'd guess.

scenes.label: Sixty seconds
scenes.say: Number five. A mockingbird can learn your face in about a minute.

scenes.label: Florida, 2009
scenes.say: In 2009, biologist Doug Levey at the University of Florida tried something sneaky on a huge, busy campus.

scenes.label: 51,000 students
scenes.say: That campus had more than fifty-one thousand students. So these birds see thousands of faces every single day.

scenes.label: 24 nests
scenes.say: Ten student volunteers visited twenty-four mockingbird nests. Each one walked up, reached in, touched the edge of the nest, and walked away.

scenes.label: Four days
scenes.say: Same volunteer, same nest, four days in a row. And they changed their clothes and their path every time.

scenes.label: Getting angrier
scenes.say: By day three, the birds flew off sooner. More alarm calls. Some even swooped down and grazed people's heads.

scenes.label: Day five
scenes.say: Then on day five, a brand new volunteer walked up. And the birds barely reacted. They waited until the last moment.

scenes.label: Not all equal
scenes.say: Levey put it simply. Mockingbirds do not see all humans as equal. Sixty seconds of exposure was all it took.

scenes.label: Think about that
scenes.say: Think about that. Out of fifty-one thousand people, the bird picked out the few who bothered it. Okay, but what about pigeons?

scenes.label: Coat swap
scenes.say: Number four. Pigeons see right through your disguise.

scenes.label: Paris, 2011
scenes.say: In 2011, Dalila Bovet's team in Paris worked with wild city pigeons in a park. No training. Just regular pigeons.

scenes.label: Two researchers
scenes.say: Two women researchers, similar age, similar build, wore lab coats in different colors. Both of them fed the pigeons.

scenes.label: Kind vs mean
scenes.say: But here's the twist. One of them fed the birds and then ignored them. The other one fed them, and then chased them away.

scenes.label: Still avoided
scenes.say: Later, nobody chased anybody. And the pigeons still kept away from the one who'd been mean.

scenes.label: Swapped coats
scenes.say: So the researchers swapped coats. That should fool a bird, right? Those coats covered about ninety percent of their bodies.

scenes.label: Not fooled
scenes.say: It didn't work. The pigeons still avoided the same woman. Bovet said they very likely recognized the researchers by their faces.

scenes.label: Life with humans
scenes.say: Why would a pigeon learn faces at all? The team thinks it comes from a long history next to people, from early domestication to busy cities.

scenes.label: Eyes on you
scenes.say: And it's not only faces. In 2009, Auguste Bayern at the University of Oxford found that hand-raised jackdaws pay attention to human eyes.

scenes.label: Slower to eat
scenes.say: When an unfamiliar person was watching, the jackdaws were slower to go for their food. Bayern said they seem to interpret human eyes as eyes.

scenes.label: Remember this
scenes.say: So that pigeon you shooed off a bench last week? Yeah. It might remember. But pigeons live with us. What about birds that almost never see people?

scenes.label: Wrong hat
scenes.say: Number three. Some birds can pick you out after a few meetings, even when someone else is wearing your hat.

scenes.label: Seoul
scenes.say: Won Young Lee was a student at Seoul National University, studying magpie nests right in the city.

scenes.label: Scolded
scenes.say: And the magpies started following him. Scolding him. Even dive-bombing him when he came back.

scenes.label: Cap trick
scenes.say: So he tried a trick. He gave his cap to another person. The magpie ignored the cap and followed Lee.

scenes.label: Same clothes
scenes.say: Then his team tested two people in the same clothes. One climbed to the nests, one didn't. All the magpies went after the climber. None went after the other person.

scenes.label: Antarctica
scenes.say: Okay, but magpies live in a city full of people. So years later, Lee tried it somewhere with almost no humans. Antarctica.

scenes.label: Brown skua
scenes.say: On King George Island lives a big, tough seabird called the brown skua. It's so bold it steals food from other birds.

scenes.label: Milk thief
scenes.say: It even steals milk from nursing elephant seals. Seriously. That's a real thing researchers have described.

scenes.label: Seven nests
scenes.say: Lee's team checked seven skua nests once a week. And after just three or four visits, the skuas knew exactly who they were.

scenes.label: 7 out of 7
scenes.say: In the test, a nest visitor and a neutral person walked toward the nests, then split up. All seven skua pairs chased the nest visitor. None chased the other person.

scenes.label: Any outfit
scenes.say: One researcher, Yeong-Deok Han, even changed his field clothes. He said the birds seemed to know him no matter what he wore.

scenes.label: No humans before
scenes.say: And here's what's wild. These birds evolved where there were no humans at all. People only showed up when research stations were built.

scenes.label: The grudge
scenes.say: Number two. And this one is the scariest. Crows don't just recognize you. They hold a grudge, and they spread the word.

scenes.label: Seattle, 2006
scenes.say: Around Valentine's Day in 2006, John Marzluff's team at the University of Washington put on rubber masks.

scenes.label: Caveman mask
scenes.say: One mask was an ugly caveman face. Wearing it, they trapped seven crows on campus, banded their legs, and let them go within minutes.

scenes.label: Control mask
scenes.say: The other mask was a face of Dick Cheney, the vice president back then. That mask never trapped anything.

scenes.label: 31 crows
scenes.say: Two days later, a researcher walked past thirty-one crows in the caveman mask. Three of them scolded him.

scenes.label: Never trapped
scenes.say: But here's the twist. One of those angry crows had never been trapped at all. It likely learned that face secondhand.

scenes.label: Word spreads
scenes.say: Over the next years, many of the scolding crows had no leg bands. Crows that were never caught were learning the face from others.

scenes.label: Hawk-level threat
scenes.say: And here's the creepy part. The crows scolded that caveman the way they scold a hawk or a raccoon. The bigger the threat, the more intense the scolding.

scenes.label: 47 of 53
scenes.say: On one walk, Marzluff wore the caveman mask and met fifty-three crows. Forty-seven of them scolded him.

scenes.label: Cheney ignored
scenes.say: And the Dick Cheney mask? Mostly ignored. The crows didn't hate masks. They hated that one face.

scenes.label: Peak in 2013
scenes.say: The angry calls peaked around 2013, seven years after the trapping. Then, slowly, they faded.

scenes.label: 17 years
scenes.say: Finally, in September 2023, seventeen years after it started, a masked walk went by with no scolding crow at all.

scenes.label: Seventeen years
scenes.say: Seventeen years of grudge. Now, what could possibly top that? Here's the one I promised you.

scenes.label: Women vs men
scenes.say: Number one. Birds are more afraid of women than men. And nobody knows why.

scenes.label: This week
scenes.say: This study made headlines this week. It's in the journal People and Nature, from a team led by Federico Morelli at the University of Turin.

scenes.label: 5 countries
scenes.say: They worked in city parks and green spaces in five countries. Czechia, France, Germany, Poland and Spain.

scenes.label: 37 species
scenes.say: They tested thirty-seven bird species. Great tits, house sparrows, blackbirds, magpies, pigeons.

scenes.label: 2,701 tests
scenes.say: Men and women, matched for height and clothes, walked straight toward the birds. Two thousand seven hundred and one times.

scenes.label: How close?
scenes.say: Each time, they measured how close the person got before the bird flew off. Scientists call it flight initiation distance.

scenes.label: About 1 meter
scenes.say: And men could get about one meter closer than women, on average. Same clothes, same height. Different result.

scenes.label: Every species
scenes.say: And it wasn't one weird bird. The pattern showed up in all five countries and in all thirty-seven species.

scenes.label: Can't explain
scenes.say: Daniel Blumstein from UCLA, one of the authors, said the results are convincing. And then he said, I can't explain them right now.

scenes.label: Three guesses
scenes.say: So what's going on? The team has three guesses. Maybe scent, like pheromones. Maybe body shape. Or maybe the way men and women walk.

scenes.label: Not neutral
scenes.say: Yanina Benedetti, a woman on the team, said she was surprised. Lots of studies assume the human watching the birds is neutral. Maybe we're not.

scenes.label: Still a mystery
scenes.say: The team calls it preliminary. They want new tests that pull scent, shape, and walking apart. So for now, it's a real mystery.

scenes.label: They're watching
scenes.say: So. Mockingbirds learn your face in a minute. Pigeons see through a coat swap. Skuas learned us fast. Crows remember for seventeen years.

scenes.label: Your guess?
scenes.say: And somehow, birds treat women and men differently, and nobody knows how. What's your guess? Scent, shape, or the walk? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: Crows Can Remember Your Face for 17 Years
short.header: Birds secretly know who you are
short.description: Crows held a grudge against one mask for 17 years, and taught it to crows that were never caught. This week, a study found city birds flee sooner from women than men. Sources: University of Washington (Marzluff), People and Nature (Morelli et al.).

scenes.say: Crows can remember your face for seventeen years. And they'll tell their friends.
In 2006, scientists in Seattle trapped seven crows while wearing a scary caveman mask. Then they let them go.
Soon, crows that were never caught started screaming at that mask too. The warning spread.
On one walk, forty-seven out of fifty-three crows scolded the mask. The scolding only stopped seventeen years later.
And this week, scientists showed birds in five countries flee sooner from women than from men. Nobody knows why.
Pigeons see right through a coat swap. And mockingbirds learn a face in about a minute.
So be nice to the bird outside your window. Because remember,
